name: Erik Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Erik. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior copywriter at Barkley's, a pet-food brand, and I lead the campaigns for the dog range. Most days I'm writing pack copy, shelf talkers, the little cards in pet shops, and planning the next season's ads with the brand manager. I still write the way I was taught, on a blank page with a coffee, no software helping. I don't use AI at all, I just don't trust what comes out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How's the company doing, and how are things for you money-wise?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Barkley's got bought last spring by Norvale Foods, a much bigger group, and there's been talk of merging our marketing with theirs in the city. I live on my own in a flat above a hardware shop, I've got a car loan, and I've maybe three weeks of money put aside. There's not much else round here for a copywriter, so if Barkley's goes, I'd be driving an hour each way or moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. I never bought the hype anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, a useful bit of kit and nothing more. At work I'd make the point that our best pack copy still comes from people who own dogs. I'm not one for posting online, so that's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, AI isn't my main worry, the takeover is. Norvale could merge us into their city team whether or not AI is any good. Even with AI fizzling out, I'm one memo away from a long commute or a redundancy letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do good work, so I'm the obvious one to keep. I'd stop eating out and put an extra fifty a week aside, and I'd cancel the car upgrade I was looking at. Then I'd wait for Norvale to show its hand before doing anything bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit tired of waiting. The AI news wouldn't be the thing keeping me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the merger memo came next month, what's your first move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask straight out whether there's a role in the city and what it pays. If it covers the fuel, I'd probably take it. I'm not one to jump ship without something solid to land on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at Barkley's you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gail on the brand side, she's been there twenty years and she's got a mortgage. And our designer, who's younger than me. Merging teams always means someone's chair goes.

say: I'd say AI turned out to be a **useful bit of kit** and nothing more.
I'd point out our best pack copy comes from **dog owners**, not software.
think: The **Norvale takeover** worries me more than AI does.
I'm one memo from a **long commute** or a redundancy letter.
do: Keep my head down and do **good work** so I'm the obvious keep.
Put an **extra fifty** a week aside and drop the car upgrade.
Wait for **Norvale** to show its hand before acting.
feel: **Uneasy** and tired of waiting on the merger news.
S0.quote: Even with AI fizzling out, I'm one memo away from a long commute or a redundancy letter.
fieldNote: His real pressure is an **ownership change**, not technology.
He's **cautious by habit** and won't move without something solid.
He thinks of **colleagues** with more at stake than him.

steps.text: Keep writing the dog-range pack copy at Barkley's
Put an extra fifty a week aside and drop the car upgrade
Wait for Norvale's merger decision before job hunting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the one I'd worry about. Writing's right at the front of that list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's a sensible middle, use it for the dull stuff and keep people for the brand voice. At work I'd keep it measured, I don't want to look like a dinosaur. To friends I'd say it's going to be a rough few years for writers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm in trouble in this one. I've never used these tools and Norvale will already have a team in the city that does. If they merge us and one side knows the software and the other side doesn't, I know which side goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably have to learn the basics, even though I don't want to. Maybe a free online course over the winter. I'd also update my CV and look at copy jobs in the city, an hour's drive, and work out if the fuel makes it worth it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying in bed doing sums about fuel and rent. Not using AI at work feels like being the last one still using a paper map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the basics even though you don't want to. What's stopping you now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stubbornness, mostly. I like knowing every word came from me. I'm not proud of it, but I've been putting it off for two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you had to cut back, what goes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car loan is the big one, so I'd look at selling and getting something older outright. Then the football season ticket, which hurts. I'd keep the rent paid before anything else.

say: I'd say use AI for the **dull stuff** and keep people for the brand voice.
I'd tell friends it's a **rough few years** for writers.
think: I've **never used** the tools, and Norvale's city team already does.
If one side knows the software, I know **which side goes**.
do: Take a **free online course** on the basics over the winter.
Update my CV and look at **city copy jobs** an hour away.
Sell the car and buy **something older** outright.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake doing sums about fuel and rent.
S1.quote: Not using AI at work feels like being the last one still using a paper map.
fieldNote: He clearly sees the **merger plus AI** as a double threat.
He admits his refusal is **stubbornness**, not principle.
His public tone stays **measured** to avoid looking old-fashioned.

steps.text: Take a free online course on AI writing basics this winter
Apply for copywriting jobs in the city an hour away
Sell the car on finance and buy an older one outright
Give up the football season ticket

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's... I wouldn't know where to start, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say the government needs to slow it down somehow, give people time. I'm not usually one for big government stuff, but that'd be too fast for anyone. At work I'd just say nobody knows what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be finished as a copywriter by about 2029. My job is all thinking work, so the three-year gap before robots doesn't help me at all. I've got no savings to speak of, no AI skills, and nothing lined up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't really know. I'd probably ring my parents and ask if I could move back for a bit to stop paying rent. I'd take whatever job came up, warehouse, delivery, anything with hours, while those still need people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicked, if I'm honest. Like the ground's gone soft and I can't see where to put my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said warehouse or delivery. Would you really do that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to. My dad drove a van for thirty years. At twenty-nine I'd be asking my dad how to get a van licence, which isn't where I thought a master's degree would get me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents when you called?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it's temporary. They'd know it wasn't. My mum would make up the spare room and not say anything, which would be worse.

say: I'd say the government should **slow it down** and give people time.
At work I'd just say **nobody knows** what's coming.
think: I'd be finished as a copywriter **by 2029**.
With no savings or **AI skills**, I'd have nothing lined up.
do: Ring my parents and ask to **move back** home.
Take any job with hours, like **warehouse or delivery** work.
feel: **Panicked**, like the ground has gone soft.
S2.quote: At twenty-nine I'd be asking my dad how to get a van licence, which isn't where I thought a master's degree would get me.
fieldNote: He has **no plan** and says so plainly.
His fallback is his **dad's trade**, which hurts his pride.
A centrist by habit, he still wants government to **slow things down**.

steps.text: Move back into his parents' spare room to stop paying rent
Lean on his parents for food and housing while he looks
Get a van licence and take delivery or warehouse work
Back calls for the government to slow the rollout

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Better. Still not much if you're starting from nothing like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get people retrained if firms and government actually do something. I'd say it at work, sensibly, and probably nowhere else. I'm not a campaigner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be gone from Barkley's by 2031, probably sooner if Norvale merges us. What I know is pets and the people who buy for them. I've thought before about dog grooming, which is hands-on, and robots for that are years after 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time grooming course in the first year, about nine hundred, paid in instalments. I'd keep my job and save hard, maybe forty a week. I'd ask the grooming salon on the high street if I could help on Saturdays to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still frightened, but less frozen. Having one thing to aim at helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: That's a big change from copywriting. Does it suit you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More than you'd think. I like dogs more than meetings. Grooming a nervous spaniel on a Saturday morning sounds better than a merger call with a head office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the money while you train?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight. The course and the car loan together would wipe out any savings. I'd have to hope Barkley's keeps me long enough to finish.

say: I'd say five years is enough to **retrain people** if firms and government act.
I'd say it **at work**, sensibly, and nowhere else.
think: I'd be gone from Barkley's **by 2031**, maybe sooner.
**Dog grooming** is hands-on, so robots reach it years later.
do: Start a part-time **grooming course**, about nine hundred in instalments.
Save about **forty a week** while keeping my job.
Help at the **high-street salon** on Saturdays to learn.
feel: Frightened but **less frozen**, with one thing to aim at.
S3.quote: Grooming a nervous spaniel on a Saturday morning sounds better than a merger call with a head office.
fieldNote: Five years lets a **resistant** person pick one concrete escape.
He chooses a **hands-on trade** near his own brand's world.
His savings are so thin the course **wipes them out**.

steps.text: Start a part-time dog-grooming course paid in instalments
Help at the high-street grooming salon on Saturdays
Save about forty a week toward course fees
Keep his Barkley's job as long as Norvale allows

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's a long way off. I'd be thirty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if people are sensible about it. No need to panic. I'd probably say that to my mates down the pub too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I'd do nothing for a while, I know myself. The merger's the nearer worry anyway. I'd probably stay a copywriter as long as someone pays me and look at grooming in five years or so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd keep working, pay down the car loan and maybe start saving properly. I'd keep an eye on what Norvale does. I'd probably not touch the AI stuff unless I was told to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A low hum of worry. Not scary yet, just there in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any risk in waiting five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, obviously. By 2036 everyone and their cousin will be trying to get into something hands-on, but I've never been one to move early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Norvale merged the teams next year anyway, would that change things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would. If they cut me next year, I'd go straight for the grooming course and stop pretending. The merger would make the decision for me.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time** if people are sensible.
I'd tell mates at the pub there's **no need to panic**.
think: Ten years means I'd **do nothing** for a while, and I know myself.
The **merger** stays the nearer worry, so grooming waits five years.
do: Keep working and **pay down** the car loan.
Keep watching **Norvale's** plans for the team.
Avoid **AI tools** unless told to use them.
feel: A **low hum** of worry in the background.
S4.quote: By 2036 everyone and their cousin will be trying to get into something hands-on, but I've never been one to move early.
fieldNote: More time makes him **more passive**, and he admits it.
His real trigger is still the **Norvale** decision.
He sees the **crowding risk** of waiting but accepts it.

steps.text: Keep writing for Barkley's and pay down the car loan
Carry on without AI tools until told otherwise
Wait to see if Norvale merges the marketing teams

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd have no money, no plan and no skills for it. What would help is a decent wage while I retrain in something hands-on, and the course costs covered. Living near my parents would help too, I suppose.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the takeovers. Everyone's talking about AI. A big company buying a small one does the same thing to people like me as AI, just with a nicer press release.

headlineQuote: A big company buying a small one does the same thing to people like me as AI, just with a nicer press release.
portrait: Erik is a **27-year-old** senior copywriter at a pet-food brand who never uses AI.
He lives alone with a **car loan** and about three weeks of savings.
A recent **takeover** by a bigger group worries him more than AI.
In fast pictures he has **no plan** and would move back to his parents.
Given five years he'd aim for **dog grooming**, a hands-on trade.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd have no money, plan or skills for it.
whatWouldHelp: A **decent wage** while he retrains in a hands-on trade, with course costs covered.
